findings.step: main answer box (every problem in the lesson)
findings.why: Every question in this lesson asks for an angle, and every main-box unit is configured as '(none)'. A struggling student moving through problem after problem gets no visual cue in the box itself confirming a bare number (not '62°') is wanted. The walk's arithmetic lines ('124 ÷ 2 = ') do model bare numbers, which softens the risk, but nothing next to the input ever states 'degrees'.
findings.fix: Add a 'degrees' (or '°') unit tag to the main answer box for every circle-theorem problem, or add a short instruction line like 'Give your answer in degrees, no ° symbol needed.'

findings.step: ask[0]: 'How many circumference angles make the centre angle? Type the multiplier:'
findings.why: The phrasing inverts the natural direction of the relationship the intro just gave ('centre is twice circumference'), asking instead 'how many circumference angles make the centre angle' — a convoluted double-negative-feeling construction for a struggling reader to parse.
findings.fix: Reword to match the intro's direction, e.g. 'The centre angle is how many times the circumference angle? Type the multiplier:' (later problems like bronze[1]/bronze[6] already use clearer versions of this step).

findings.step: ask[0]: 'A diameter is a straight line. How many degrees is a straight line?'
findings.why: Minor grammatical awkwardness ('how many degrees is a straight line' rather than 'are in'); understandable but reads slightly off.
findings.fix: Reword to 'How many degrees are there in a straight line?'

findings.step: ask[2]: 'Check the pair match: 35 and  [box expects 35]'
findings.why: The sentence is a dangling fragment — 'Check the pair match: 35 and ___' does not say what relationship the student is confirming or what to type. A struggling student can't tell if they should re-type 35, type a different value, or answer yes/no.
findings.fix: Complete the sentence, e.g. 'Check the pair match — type the other angle: 35 and ___ should be equal.'

findings.step: ask[2]: 'Check the pair are equal: 64 and  [box expects 64]'
findings.why: Same dangling-fragment pattern as bronze[4] — '64 and ___' gives no instruction for what the blank represents.
findings.fix: Reword to 'The alternate segment angle should also be 64°. Type it to check: ___'

findings.step: ask[2]: 'Check the pair match: 12 and  [box expects 12]'
findings.why: Same recurring fragment. Additionally this is the one problem in the lesson where the answer is a length (TB = 12 cm, matching the given TA = 12 cm) rather than an angle, so the missing unit label is slightly more exposed here than in the angle-only problems.
findings.fix: Reword the fragment as above, and consider showing 'cm' on this box since TA was explicitly given in cm.

findings.step: ask[2]: 'Check the pair match: 70 and  [box expects 70]'
findings.why: Same recurring dangling-fragment pattern (4th occurrence in this lesson: bronze[4], silver[1], silver[3], gold[2]) — worth fixing once as a template rather than per-instance.
findings.fix: Standardise the 'check the pair' step wording across the lesson, e.g. 'ABT should equal 70° too. Type it: ___'

findings.step: ask[1]: 'So 50 = x, meaning x =  [box expects 50]'
findings.why: Slightly circular/redundant phrasing — it states '50 = x' and then immediately re-asks for x, which a struggling reader may find confusing about whether new work is required.
findings.fix: Reword to 'So x = 50. Type x:' or simply drop the restated box since the previous line already gives the value.

findings.step: ask[2]: 'C is on the minor arc, so use the reflex angle: 360 − 110 ='
findings.why: Relies on the student already grasping why a point on the minor arc subtends the reflex (not the normal) centre angle — a well-known GCSE trouble spot. The intro asserts this but doesn't build the visual/conceptual reasoning, only the arithmetic consequence.
findings.fix: Add a short visual or one-line explanation before this step, e.g. 'C sits on the short arc, on the far side from the 110° angle, so it "sees" the rest of the circle — the reflex angle.'

findings.step: final ask: 'Now multiply by the height: 24 × 3 =  [box expects 72]'
findings.why: This is the actual volume answer (cuboid volume) but the box carries no unit. In an exam a bare '72' without cm³ loses a mark; the box gives no cue that a unit is/isn't wanted.
findings.fix: Label this box 'cm³', or add 'Give your answer in cm³' to the question stem.

findings.step: ask[1]/ask[2]: 'Six faces: 6 × 25 = [150]' then 'Compare: the volume would be 5 × 5 × 5 = [125]'
findings.why: Two different magnitude types (surface area, cm², vs volume, cm³) sit back-to-back with identical unlabelled boxes. A struggling student has no textual cue that 150 and 125 are fundamentally different kinds of quantity, which is exactly the cm/cm²/cm³ mix-up this lesson exists to prevent.
findings.fix: Tag each box inline, e.g. '150 cm²' and 'the volume would be … = 125 cm³', so the two magnitudes are visibly distinguished even in a 'compare' aside.

findings.step: ask[0]: 'Write the cross-section area:  [box expects 12]'
findings.why: This just restates the given 12 cm² with no unit shown; low risk since it's a direct restatement, but still an unlabelled physical quantity.
findings.fix: Label 'cm²' or skip re-asking a value already given verbatim.

findings.step: final ask: 'Multiply by the length: 12 × 10 =  [box expects 120]'
findings.why: Final volume answer, no unit cue.
findings.fix: Label 'cm³'.

findings.step: final ask: 'Multiply by π: 63 × π =  [box expects 197.9]'
findings.why: Final cylinder-volume answer, unlabelled.
findings.fix: Label 'cm³'.

findings.step: final ask: 'Divide the volume by the base area: 180 ÷ 45 =  [box expects 4]'
findings.why: Unlike almost every other problem in this lesson, the requested quantity here is a LENGTH (height, cm), not a volume or area — yet the box is styled identically to every volume/area box around it (same 'NO unit label'). A student pattern-matching on the rest of the lesson could misjudge what kind of number is expected here.
findings.fix: Label this box 'cm' to visually flag that this particular answer is a length, not a volume.

findings.step: ask[1]/ask[2]: 'Multiply by the side again: 16 × 4 = [64]' then 'Compare: the surface area would be 6 × 16 = [96]'
findings.why: Same area/volume mixing risk as bronze[1] — 64 (cm³, the actual answer) and 96 (cm², a distractor comparison) sit adjacent with no labels distinguishing them.
findings.fix: Tag inline: '64 cm³' and 'the surface area would be … = 96 cm²'.

findings.step: ask[0]: 'Radius = 10 ÷ 2 =  [box expects 5]'
findings.why: A length (radius, cm) mid-walk with no unit; low risk since halving a stated cm length is unambiguous in context.
findings.fix: Label 'cm' for consistency.

findings.step: final ask: 'Multiply by π: 150 × π =  [box expects 471.2]'
findings.why: Final cylinder-volume answer, unlabelled.
findings.fix: Label 'cm³'.

findings.step: final ask: 'Add the three and double: 2 × (24 + 16 + 6) =  [box expects 92]'
findings.why: Final surface-area answer, unlabelled; this problem is internally consistent (everything is cm² including the 'check' step at 46), so risk is lower than the bronze[1]/bronze[5] mixing cases, but a struggling student still doesn't know if cm² should be written.
findings.fix: Label 'cm²'.

findings.step: final ask: 'Multiply by π: 100 × π =  [box expects 314.2]'
findings.why: Final cone-volume answer, unlabelled.
findings.fix: Label 'cm³'.

findings.step: final ask: 'Multiply by π: 288 × π =  [box expects 904.8]'
findings.why: Final sphere-volume answer, unlabelled.
findings.fix: Label 'cm³'.

findings.step: final ask: 'Multiply by π: 64 × π =  [box expects 201.1]'
findings.why: Final sphere-surface-area answer, unlabelled. This problem also directly follows two volume problems (silver[0], silver[1]) with identical box styling, so there's a context-switch risk of a student carrying over 'cm³' thinking into a cm² answer.
findings.fix: Label 'cm²', and consider a brief 'this time it's area, not volume' cue given the run of volume problems just before it.

findings.step: ask[0]/ask[1]: 'In π units: 2 × 5² =  [box expects 50]' / 'Take the ends off the total: 150 − 50 =  [box expects 100]'
findings.why: This is a 'work in π units' technique where the boxed number (50, 100) is really a coefficient of π (i.e. 50 means 50π cm²), but nothing beside the box states this, and the box carries no unit at all. A struggling student can easily read '50' as a literal cm² area rather than a coefficient still needing ×π, especially since no other problem in the bronze/silver run before this one uses this shorthand.
findings.fix: Either show the working with the π explicitly retained at each line (e.g. '2 × 5² = 50π') or add a one-line reminder just above the steps: 'Every number below is really "× π" — we only multiply by π at the very end.'

findings.step: final ask: 'so 100 = 10h, h = 100 ÷ 10 =  [box expects 10]'
findings.why: Final answer here is a length (cylinder height, cm) — a different magnitude type from most of the lesson's volume/area answers — with no unit shown.
findings.fix: Label 'cm'.

findings.step: check: 'Check: 50π + 2π(5)(10) in π units is 50 + 100 =  [box expects 150]'
findings.why: Dense, run-on sentence mixing symbolic notation (50π + 2π(5)(10)) with a parenthetical qualifier ('in π units is') in a single clause — hard for a struggling reader to parse in one pass.
findings.fix: Split into two shorter lines, e.g. 'Check: 50π + 2π(5)(10) = 50π + 100π. In π units that's 50 + 100 = ___'.

findings.step: ask[0]: 'Base area (square): 6 × 6 =  [box expects 36]'
findings.why: Intermediate area (cm²) unlabelled, feeding into a volume final answer — same area-then-volume sequencing seen elsewhere in the lesson, lower risk here since there's no 'compare' distractor.
findings.fix: Label 'cm²' if labelling is added lesson-wide.

findings.step: final ask: 'Take one third: 360 ÷ 3 =  [box expects 120]'
findings.why: Final pyramid-volume answer, unlabelled.
findings.fix: Label 'cm³'.

findings.step: final ask: 'Multiply by π: 486 × π =  [box expects 1526.8]'
findings.why: Final hemisphere-volume answer, unlabelled.
findings.fix: Label 'cm³'.

findings.step: ask[0]/ask[1]: 'The r² part: 5² =  [25]' then 'Multiply both sides by 3: 150 × 3 =  [450]'
findings.why: Same 'work in π units' technique as silver[3] — the intro does explicitly prime it ('work in multiples of π to keep it exact') and the question already states volume = 150π cm³, which somewhat justifies the abstraction, but a struggling student can still lose track of what '450' represents mid-algebra.
findings.fix: Keep the intro priming (already present) but add a brief inline note at the first π-units step reminding the student these numbers are coefficients of π, not final cm values.

findings.step: final ask: 'Divide by 25: 450 ÷ 25 =  [box expects 18]'
findings.why: Final answer is a length (cone height, cm), a different magnitude type from most of the lesson, unlabelled.
findings.fix: Label 'cm'.

findings.step: ask[0]-ask[2]: 'Curved part factor…', 'Base factor…', 'Add them: 15 + 9 =  [24]'
findings.why: Another 'in π units' chain (r×l and r² as bare coefficients) without restating that these are ×π quantities until the final multiply-by-π step.
findings.fix: Same fix as silver[3]/silver[6] — an inline reminder that intermediate numbers are π-coefficients.

findings.step: final ask: 'Multiply by π: 24 × π =  [box expects 75.4]'
findings.why: Final cone total-surface-area answer, unlabelled.
findings.fix: Label 'cm²'.

findings.step: ask[0]-ask[2]: 'Big cone factor… [108]', 'Small cone factor… [4]', 'Subtract: 108 − 4 =  [104]'
findings.why: Same π-units abstraction pattern as gold[0]/silver[3]/silver[6], repeated a fourth time in this lesson without ever explaining the technique explicitly to the student (each problem just re-primes it locally).
findings.fix: Consider a single shared explainer box the first time this pattern appears in the lesson ('Working in π units' technique callout), rather than re-deriving silently each time.

findings.step: final ask: 'Multiply by π: 104 × π =  [box expects 326.7]'
findings.why: Final frustum-volume answer, unlabelled.
findings.fix: Label 'cm³'.

findings.step: ask[0]-ask[2]: 'Cylinder volume… [785.4]', 'Sphere volume… [523.6]', 'Subtract: 785.4 − 523.6 =  [261.8]'
findings.why: Three sequential cm³ values in one problem, all unlabelled — lower risk than the bronze mixing cases since all three really are the same magnitude type (volume), but still no unit cue for the actual final answer.
findings.fix: Label 'cm³' on at least the final subtraction box.

findings.step: check: 'Check: the gap is exactly a third of the cylinder, 250π/3 rounds to  [box expects 261.8]'
findings.why: Springs a general fact ('the gap is exactly a third of the cylinder') on the student with no derivation anywhere in the walk — it's mathematically true but presented as a given, which can read as an unexplained leap rather than a check.
findings.fix: Either derive it briefly ('cylinder − sphere = 2πr³ − 4/3πr³ = 2/3 of cylinder... wait check arithmetic') or drop the 'exactly a third' framing and just re-verify the subtraction a different way, e.g. recomputing from πr²(2r) − (4/3)πr³ directly.

findings.step: final ask: 'Add them: 502.7 + 134.0 =  [box expects 636.7]'
findings.why: Consistent cm³ throughout this composite-solid problem, but still no unit shown on the final total.
findings.fix: Label 'cm³'.

findings.step: check: 'Check in π units: 160 + 128/3 = 608/3, and 608π/3 rounds to  [box expects 636.7]'
findings.why: Very dense single sentence chaining two fraction manipulations and a rounding instruction — a struggling reader has to hold three sub-results in mind at once to follow it.
findings.fix: Break into two lines: 'In π units: 160 + 128/3 = 608/3.' then 'So 608π/3 rounds to ___'.

findings.step: final ask: 'Square root: √25 =  [box expects 5]'
findings.why: Final answer is a length (sphere radius, cm) — again a different magnitude type from the volume/area answers that dominate this lesson — with no unit shown.
findings.fix: Label 'cm'.
